units:
Change Management for 
Sustainability
Overcoming the barriers to implementing sustainability initiatives

Learning outcomes
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 2
■ Diagnose why sustainability initiatives stall, using a six-part barrier taxonomy.
■ Apply Kotter, Lewin and ADKAR to a real sustainability initiative.
■ Quantify a split-incentive problem, a force-field analysis and an adoption funnel.
■ Design a change plan: coalition, quick wins, incentives, nudges and KPIs.
■ Evaluate Interface, Cochin Airport and BP, and the limits of change models.

S E C T I O N 1
Why Initiatives Stall
Most organisations now say sustainability matters. The hard part is turning commitment 
into daily practice.
4

W H Y I N I T I A T I V E S S T A L L
The implementation gap
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 5
■ Commitment is high: Deloitte's 2025 global C-suite survey 
found sustainability embedded in executive priorities, yet 
impact still lagging.
■ Barriers it names: limited resources, policy uncertainty, 
and poor data availability and quality.
■ The core gap: many firms struggle to turn leadership 
commitments into day-to-day action.
■ Money is moving: Deloitte's 2026 survey reports most 
companies increased sustainability investment, citing 
higher returns.
S O W H A T ?
The bottleneck has shifted from 
"should we?" to "how do we 
actually get it done?" That is a 
change-management problem, 
not only a technology problem.

W H Y I N I T I A T I V E S S T A L L
The "70% of change fails" myth
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 6
70%
The statistic quoted in countless 
consulting decks and textbooks
5
Published instances Hughes (2011) 
traced and reviewed
0
Valid, reliable empirical studies he 
found supporting the figure
Change efforts do fail, but no one knows the true rate. Do not quote 70% as fact; use it only as a prompt to plan carefully.

W H Y I N I T I A T I V E S S T A L L
Why sustainability change is harder than ordinary change
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 7
Typical business change
■ Benefits land in one department
■ Payback is usually visible within a budget cycle
■ Owner and metric are clear
■ Data exists in existing systems
■ Success is judged by profit
Sustainability change
■ Benefits spread across functions and years
■ Payback may be long or indirect
■ Ownership is shared, so often no one's job
■ Data (Scope 3, water, waste) is immature
■ Success mixes cost, risk, reputation and ethics

W H Y I N I T I A T I V E S S T A L L
A six-part barrier taxonomy
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 8
Strategic & leadership
No clear target, weak sponsorship, 
sustainability seen as a side project.
Structural
Silos, unclear ownership, no cross￾functional forum.
Financial
Upfront cost, short payback hurdles, 
split incentives.
Data & measurement
Poor baselines, inconsistent metrics, 
weak supplier data.
Cultural & behavioural
Habit, status-quo bias, scepticism, 
"not my job".
External & policy
Shifting regulation, weak 
infrastructure, supply chain limits.

W H Y I N I T I A T I V E S S T A L L
Strategic and leadership barriers
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 9
■ Vague ambition: "Be greener" with no baseline, target, 
owner or budget.
■ Weak sponsorship: a CEO announcement, but no senior 
leader whose pay or promotion depends on delivery.
■ Side-project status: the sustainability team reports far 
from where capital and operations decisions are made.
■ Short-termism: quarterly results crowd out multi-year 
investments.
■ Skills gap: managers lack the capability to run 
decarbonisation projects.
D I A G N O S T I C Q U E S T I O N
If the sustainability lead left 
tomorrow, would the initiative 
continue? If not, it is not yet 
embedded in the business.

W H Y I N I T I A T I V E S S T A L L
Structural barriers: silos and unclear ownership
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 10
■ Cross-cutting by nature: procurement, facilities, product, finance and IT each hold one piece of 
the problem.
■ Nobody owns the whole: each function optimises its own budget and KPI.
■ Handoff failures: targets set centrally are not translated into plant-level or team-level plans.
■ Slow decisions: approvals pass through many committees, so pilots die in the queue.
■ Fix direction: cross-functional steering group, named owners, targets cascaded into each unit.

W H Y I N I T I A T I V E S S T A L L
Financial barriers: cost, payback and split incentives
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 11
■ Upfront capital: efficiency projects compete with growth 
projects that promise higher returns.
■ Hurdle rates: firms demand payback of 2-3 years even 
when 10-year savings are large.
■ Split incentives: the unit that pays for the upgrade is not 
the one that enjoys the lower bill.
■ Hidden benefits: risk reduction, talent retention and brand 
value rarely appear in the spreadsheet.
■ Fix direction: life-cycle costing, internal carbon price, 
shared-savings or green-fund mechanisms.
E N E R G Y - E F F I C I E N C Y G A P
Many efficiency measures with 
attractive returns are still not 
adopted. Cost is only part of the 
story; incentives and attention 
matter too.

W H Y I N I T I A T I V E S S T A L L
Worked example: a split incentive on campus
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 12
PROBLEM A campus replaces 2,000 tube lights (36 W) with LEDs (18 W). Use 3,000 h/yr, tariff Rs 8/kWh, cost Rs 450 per fitting 
(illustrative figures), 5 years, 12% discount rate.
1. Power saved = 2,000 x (36 - 18) W = 36,000 W = 36 kW
2. Energy saved = 36 kW x 3,000 h = 108,000 kWh per year
3. Annual saving = 108,000 x Rs 8 = Rs 8.64 lakh
4. Capital cost = 2,000 x Rs 450 = Rs 9.0 lakh; simple payback = 9.0 / 8.64 = 1.04 years
5. PV of 5 years of savings = 8.64 x 3.605 (annuity factor) = Rs 31.1 lakh; NPV = 31.1 - 9.0 = Rs 22.1 lakh
6. The barrier: if the department budget pays Rs 9 lakh but the central estate pays the bill, the department sees only cost.
Strong economics, yet it stalls. The fix is organisational: pool budgets or share savings.

W H Y I N I T I A T I V E S S T A L L
Data and measurement barriers
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 13
■ No baseline: you cannot show progress without a starting point.
■ Inconsistent metrics: different units and boundaries make results incomparable across sites.
■ Scope 3 opacity: supplier and customer emissions are estimated, not metered.
■ Manual collection: spreadsheets and email chains breed errors and delay.
■ Consequence: leaders do not trust the numbers, so they do not fund or act on them.
■ Fix direction: start with a few reliable metrics, automate data capture, assign data owners.

W H Y I N I T I A T I V E S S T A L L
Cultural and behavioural barriers
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 14
Status-quo bias
People prefer the familiar. "We have 
always done it this way."
Present bias
Costs are now, benefits later, so 
action keeps getting postponed.
Loss aversion
Giving up a convenience feels larger 
than an equal gain.
"Not my job"
Responsibility diffuses when 
everyone is partly responsible.
Cynicism
Past greenwashing or failed 
programmes make staff discount 
new ones.
Change fatigue
Too many parallel initiatives exhaust 
attention and goodwill.

W H Y I N I T I A T I V E S S T A L L
External and policy barriers
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 15
■ Regulatory uncertainty: fragmented or shifting rules make long investments hard to plan.
■ Infrastructure limits: weak grid, no recycling system or no charging network outside the firm's 
control.
■ Supplier readiness: small suppliers lack data, capital or skills to follow your targets.
■ Market signals: customers say they want green products but may not pay a premium.
■ Response: scenario planning, industry coalitions, supplier support programmes, policy 
engagement.

W H Y I N I T I A T I V E S S T A L L
Activity: sort the barrier
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 16
Place each statement into the barrier family that best fits. Discuss in pairs for 3 minutes.
Strategic / Structural
Targets, sponsorship, ownership, silos, 
decision paths
Financial / Data
Cost, payback, incentives, baselines, 
metrics
Cultural / External
Habits, trust, regulation, infrastructure, 
suppliers
1. "The CEO announced net zero but nobody's bonus depends on it."
2. "Facilities pays for the chillers; the departments pay the power bill."
3. "Our site data is in five different spreadsheet formats."
4. "Staff roll their eyes; last year's green drive just vanished."
5. "The state recycling facility is 400 km away."
6. "Procurement and design never talk to each other."

W H Y I N I T I A T I V E S S T A L L
Quick check 1
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 17
According to Hughes (2011), what is the evidence for the claim that 70% of organisational change initiatives 
fail?
A A. Strong: it comes from many large randomised studies
B B. Mixed: some studies support it, some contradict it
C C. None valid or reliable: the figure lacks empirical support
D D. It was proven for sustainability initiatives only
Think, vote, then discuss. (Answer in speaker notes.)

W H Y I N I T I A T I V E S S T A L L
Quick check 1: answer
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 18
Answer: C. No valid, reliable empirical support
Hughes (2011) examined five published uses of the 70% figure and found no empirical basis. Lesson: be sceptical of 
precise-sounding statistics. Failure of change efforts is common and real, but its true rate is unknown, so plan for risk 
without quoting a made-up number.

S E C T I O N 2
Frameworks for Leading Change
Three classic models give you a vocabulary for diagnosing a stalled initiative and 
choosing the next move.
19

F R A M E W O R K S F O R L E A D I N G C H A N G E
What is change management?
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 20
■ Definition: the structured approach to moving people, teams and organisations from a current 
state to a desired future state.
■ Technical change: install the solar panels, change the process. The solution is known.
■ Adaptive change: people must alter habits, values and relationships. No quick fix exists.
■ Sustainability is mostly adaptive: the technology often exists; behaviour, incentives and power 
structures are the obstacle.
■ Two sides: the project side (scope, schedule, budget) and the people side (adoption, trust, 
habits).

F R A M E W O R K S F O R L E A D I N G C H A N G E
Kotter's 8 steps
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 21
1. Create urgency
Make the case for acting 
now.
2. Build a coalition
Assemble a guiding team 
with influence.
3. Form a vision
A clear picture of the future 
and strategy.
4. Communicate
Enlist volunteers with a 
simple, repeated message.
5. Remove obstacles
Clear barriers; empower 
action.
6. Quick wins
Plan and celebrate visible 
short-term wins.
7. Build on gains
Do not declare victory too 
early.
8. Anchor in 
culture
Embed new practices in 
norms and systems.

F R A M E W O R K S F O R L E A D I N G C H A N G E
Kotter applied to a campus net-zero programme
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 22
Step What it looks like in practice
Urgency Share the campus energy bill, emissions trend and regulatory outlook with leadership
Coalition Dean, estates head, finance officer, student leaders, two respected faculty
Vision "A campus that cuts its electricity emissions by half in five years while saving money"
Communicate Monthly dashboards, hostel competitions, town halls, simple slogans
Obstacles Pool the energy budget, simplify procurement for efficiency items
Quick wins LED retrofit in two blocks, visible savings in the first quarter
Build on gains Extend to HVAC, rooftop solar and hostels
Anchor Green procurement policy, energy KPIs in building managers' reviews

F R A M E W O R K S F O R L E A D I N G C H A N G E
Lewin: unfreeze, change, refreeze
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 23
Unfreeze
Create readiness. Show why the current state is 
unsustainable and lower anxiety about the move.
Change
Move to new behaviours and processes, with 
training, support and experimentation.
Refreeze
Stabilise the new state with policies, incentives, 
routines and feedback.
Critique: real organisations rarely sit still, so treat refreeze as "make the new way the default" rather than "stop changing".

F R A M E W O R K S F O R L E A D I N G C H A N G E
Worked example: force-field analysis (Lewin)
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 24
PROBLEM Should a firm launch a plant-wide energy-management system? Score each force from 1 (weak) to 5 (strong).
Driving forces: regulation 4, cost savings 4, customer demand 3, employee pride 2 = 13
Restraining forces: upfront cost 4, no reliable data 3, time on shop floor 3, scepticism 3, silos 2 = 15
Net = 13 - 15 = -2, so the change is likely to stall as designed.
Strategy: reducing restraining forces is usually cheaper than pushing harder on driving forces.
Action: run a 3-month pilot (scepticism 3 to 1) and install sub-meters (data 3 to 1).
New restraining total = 4 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 2 = 11, so net = 13 - 11 = +2.
Same drivers, but the change moves from -2 to +2 by addressing resistance, not pushing harder.

F R A M E W O R K S F O R L E A D I N G C H A N G E
Prosci ADKAR: change at the individual level
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 25
Awareness
Of the need for 
change
Desire
To support and take 
part
Knowledge
Of how to change
Ability
To implement skills 
and behaviours
Reinforcement
To sustain the 
change

F R A M E W O R K S F O R L E A D I N G C H A N G E
Using ADKAR as a diagnostic
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 26
Symptom you observe Likely gap Intervention
"Why are we doing this?" Awareness Share data and the business case; explain the why repeatedly
"I get it, but it is not my problem." Desire Link to personal goals, involve staff, address what they lose
"I do not know how to do this." Knowledge Training, guides, worked examples
"I tried but the tools do not work." Ability Coaching, time to practise, fix process and tools
"It lasted a month, then people drifted 
back." Reinforcement Recognition, KPIs, defaults, manager follow-up

F R A M E W O R K S F O R L E A D I N G C H A N G E
Resistance: enemy or information?
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 27
Resistance as enemy
■ Overcome it with a stronger push
■ Label sceptics as "blockers"
■ Communicate only benefits
■ Result: compliance without commitment
Resistance as information
■ Ask what the person is protecting
■ Often points to real design flaws
■ Involve critics in solving the issue
■ Result: a better plan and real buy-in

F R A M E W O R K S F O R L E A D I N G C H A N G E
Stakeholder map: power and interest
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 28
Group Power / interest Engagement approach
Senior leadership, CFO High / varies Manage closely: business case, risk framing, KPIs
Facility and plant managers High / high Co-design the plan; they carry the delivery
Finance and procurement Medium / low Show how rules (hurdle rates, tenders) block the goal
Employees, students Low / medium Inform, involve, give feedback and recognition
Suppliers, regulators, community Varies Collaborate, monitor, support capability

F R A M E W O R K S F O R L E A D I N G C H A N G E
Comparing the three models
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 29
Model Level Strength Limitation
Kotter 8 steps Organisation Practical sequence for large 
programmes
Linear; little on individual adoption
Lewin Organisation / group Simple; force-field analysis is a quick 
diagnostic Static view of a fluid world
ADKAR Individual Pinpoints where a person or team is 
stuck Less on strategy and power politics
Use them together: Kotter to plan, Lewin to diagnose forces, ADKAR to check people.

F R A M E W O R K S F O R L E A D I N G C H A N G E
Quick check 2
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 30
Staff understand why the new waste-sorting scheme matters and know how to do it, but still do not follow it. 
Which ADKAR element is most likely missing?
A A. Awareness
B B. Desire
C C. Knowledge
D D. Reinforcement only
Think, vote, then discuss. (Answer in speaker notes.)

F R A M E W O R K S F O R L E A D I N G C H A N G E
Quick check 2: answer
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 31
Answer: B. Desire
They are aware and they know how, so the problem is motivation. Respond by asking what they lose or fear, linking the 
scheme to their own goals, involving them in design, and fixing any convenience problems. More training or posters 
would not help here.

S E C T I O N 3
Leading Change in Practice
Plans do not fail on paper. They fail in meeting rooms, budgets and daily habits. This 
section is about the practical moves.
32

L E A D I N G C H A N G E I N P R A C T I C E
Build the case and tell the story
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 33
■ Speak each audience's language: cost and risk for finance, 
brand and growth for marketing, uptime for operations.
■ Pair numbers with a narrative: a clear "from-to" story 
people can repeat.
■ Be honest about trade-offs: name what will get harder 
and what will be given up.
■ Use life-cycle costs: show total cost of ownership, not only 
purchase price.
■ Make the first step small: a specific, easy ask beats a 
grand vision.
T E S T Y O U R P I T C H
Can a mid-level manager explain, 
in two sentences, why the 
initiative matters and what is 
expected of them?

L E A D I N G C H A N G E I N P R A C T I C E
Coalition, sponsors and champions
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 34
Executive sponsor
Owns the target, 
unblocks budgets and 
signals priority.
Steering group
Cross-functional leaders 
who resolve conflicts 
between units.
Champion 
network
Respected people in each 
team who adapt and 
promote the change 
locally.
Feedback loops
Surveys, drop-ins and 
forums that surface 
problems early.

L E A D I N G C H A N G E I N P R A C T I C E
Sequencing: quick wins first, then scale
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 35
0-30 days
Baseline, name owners, pick 2-3 
visible pilots.
30-90 days
Deliver the first quick wins; publish 
results.
3-6 months
Fix obstacles found; extend pilots; 
align incentives.
6-12 months
Scale to more units; embed in budgets 
and policy.
A quick win must be visible, unambiguous and linked to the goal, otherwise it builds cynicism, not momentum.

L E A D I N G C H A N G E I N P R A C T I C E
Incentives: what gets rewarded gets done
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 36
Misaligned
■ Managers rewarded only for short-term cost 
cuts
■ Sustainability team measured by reports, not 
outcomes
■ Procurement paid on lowest price
■ Result: green goals lose every trade-off
Aligned
■ A share of bonus linked to emissions or 
efficiency targets
■ Cost of carbon in investment appraisal
■ Procurement scored on total cost and supplier 
data
■ Result: the green choice becomes the rational 
one

L E A D I N G C H A N G E I N P R A C T I C E
Nudges: make the right thing easy
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 37
Defaults
Double-sided printing, 
green electricity or 
vegetarian option set as 
the default.
Feedback
Show real-time energy 
use and comparison with 
similar buildings.
Social norms
Tell people what most 
colleagues already do.
Reduce friction
Put recycling bins where 
the waste is created; 
automate what you can.

L E A D I N G C H A N G E I N P R A C T I C E
Worked example: why the weakest link matters (ADKAR 
funnel)
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 38
PROBLEM A firm launches a "switch off at the end of day" programme for 1,000 employees. Share who clear each ADKAR stage: A 90%, 
D 60%, K 80%, A 75%, R 70%.
1. Sustained adoption = 0.90 x 0.60 x 0.80 x 0.75 x 0.70 = 0.2268, about 227 people (22.7%).
2. Option 1: boost Awareness from 90% to 100% (more emails): 1.00 x 0.60 x 0.80 x 0.75 x 0.70 = 25.2%.
3. Option 2: boost Desire from 60% to 80% (involve staff, address concerns): 0.90 x 0.80 x 0.80 x 0.75 x 0.70 = 30.2%.
4. Same effort, but fixing the weakest stage gives +7.5 points versus +2.5 points for the strongest stage.
5. Caveat: stages are not truly independent; this is a model for prioritising, not a forecast.
Spend effort where the funnel narrows most, not where it is easiest to act.

L E A D I N G C H A N G E I N P R A C T I C E
Case: Interface and Mission Zero
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 39
L E A D E R S H I P C O N V I C T I O N O V E R 2 5 Y E A R S
■ 1994: founder Ray Anderson has his "spear in the chest" moment and 
commits the carpet maker to zero negative impact by 2020.
■ Mission Zero set aggressive targets across factories, products and supply 
chain.
■ Nov 2019: company announced success ahead of schedule.
■ Reported results: carpet carbon footprint down 74% since 1996; market￾based GHG intensity at carpet factories down 96%.
■ Successor goal: Climate Take Back, aiming to reverse global warming.
L E S S O N F O R C H A N G E L E A D E R S
A credible sponsor, a public and 
ambitious target, and persistence 
across leadership changes. Check 
how "zero" is defined before treating 
it as a model for your own claims.

L E A D I N G C H A N G E I N P R A C T I C E
Case: Cochin International Airport goes solar
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 40
S T A R T S M A L L , T H E N S C A L E
■ Started with a small 1 MW solar plant, then learned from it.
■ Aug 2015: commissioned a 12 MW solar PV plant, 46,150 panels over 18 
hectares, cost about Rs 65 crore.
■ Expected output about 18 million units a year; more than 300,000 t CO2 
avoided over 25 years.
■ Built with an engineering partner under the airport company, backed by 
state government.
■ Caveat: "fully solar" is an annual balance. The airport still uses the grid 
when the sun is down.
L E S S O N F O R C H A N G E L E A D E R S
A small pilot reduced risk and built 
confidence. A clear economic story 
(the power bill) and committed 
leadership carried the scale-up. Be 
exact about claims.

L E A D I N G C H A N G E I N P R A C T I C E
Case: BP, when commitment retreats
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 41
H O N E S T C R I T I Q U E
■ 2020: BP announced a net-zero ambition and a plan to cut oil and gas 
output by 2030 while expanding low-carbon investment.
■ 2023: the oil and gas reduction target was scaled back.
■ 2025: BP reset its strategy, cutting low-carbon spending and raising oil and 
gas investment.
■ Pressures cited: shareholder returns, share price, energy security and 
changing policy.
■ Verify the exact figures from BP's own statements before quoting.
L E S S O N F O R C H A N G E L E A D E R S
Commitments that are not anchored 
in the core business model, 
incentives and investor expectations 
can reverse. Sustainability change is 
exposed to market and political 
cycles.

L E A D I N G C H A N G E I N P R A C T I C E
Discussion: a change plan for IIT Delhi
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 42
Scenario: the Institute wants to cut hostel and lab electricity use by 30% in three years. Departments pay their own bills, 
students see no cost, and no one owns the target.
1 Which barrier families are present? Rank them.
2 Who are the key stakeholders and what does each lose?
3 Which quick win would you run in the first 90 days?
4 Which incentive or default would you change?

S E C T I O N 4
Making Change Stick
A successful pilot is not a successful change. The test is whether it survives budget cuts, 
leadership turnover and the next shiny priority.
43

M A K I N G C H A N G E S T I C K
Anchoring change in the organisation
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 44
■ Policy and procedure: revise procurement rules, travel 
policy, design standards.
■ Budgets: a dedicated, protected funding line or internal 
carbon price.
■ People systems: sustainability duties in job descriptions, 
appraisals and onboarding.
■ Governance: regular board-level review with public 
targets.
■ Culture: stories, recognition and leaders who visibly follow 
the new norms.
R E F R E E Z E
Embedding means the new way 
becomes "how we do things here" 
rather than a campaign needing 
constant energy.

M A K I N G C H A N G E S T I C K
Measuring change: leading and lagging indicators
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 45
Type Examples Use
Leading (activity) Training completion, pilots launched, suppliers with 
data, ideas submitted
Early warning on whether the change is 
taking hold
Adoption Share of units reporting data, % procurement with 
green criteria Shows behaviour actually changing
Lagging (outcome) kWh per unit, tCO2e, waste diverted, cost saved Confirms real impact and supports the 
business case
Sentiment Pulse surveys on trust, workload, change fatigue Spots resistance and fatigue before they 
harden

M A K I N G C H A N G E S T I C K
Backsliding and fatigue vs. durable change
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 46
Warning signs
■ Declaring victory after the pilot
■ Champions overloaded, no time or recognition
■ Targets met by reporting changes or offsets 
only
■ Messages repeat but nothing visibly changes
Countermeasures
■ Fix reinforcement: KPIs, defaults, manager 
follow-up
■ Reduce competing initiatives; sequence them
■ Audit data and claims to protect trust
■ Share honest progress, including setbacks

M A K I N G C H A N G E S T I C K
Critique: the limits of change-management models
C H A N G E M A N A G E M E N T F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 47
■ Evidence is thin: frameworks are popular but rigorous comparative evidence is limited, as the 
70% myth shows.
■ Power is under-weighted: models treat resistance as a communication problem; sometimes 
interests really conflict.
■ Context matters: a model tested in a corporation may not suit a university, a government or a 
village cooperative.
■ Risk of manipulation: managing people's "buy-in" can mask a poor decision; sometimes the 
initiative should change, not the people.
■ Systemic limits: one firm cannot fix prices, policy or infrastructure; collective action is also 
needed.

Engaging employees and creating a shared vision for sustainability

S E C T I O N 1
Culture and Shared Vision
Policies tell people what to do. Culture decides what they do when no one is watching.
4

C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N
What is a sustainability culture?
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 5
■ Culture: the shared values, beliefs, norms and habits that 
shape "how things are done here".
■ Sustainability culture: one where environmental and 
social impact is considered in everyday decisions, by 
everyone, without being told.
■ Not the same as: a sustainability department, a policy 
document or an annual report.
■ Why it matters: thousands of small decisions (what to buy, 
print, switch off, design) are made far from any manager.
■ Test: what happens when sustainability conflicts with a 
deadline or a cost target?
K E Y I D E A
You cannot mandate culture. You 
can shape it through leadership 
behaviour, systems and shared 
meaning.

C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N
Schein's three levels of culture
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 6
Artifacts
Visible: recycling bins, dashboards, 
dress, rituals, reports. Easy to see, 
hard to interpret.
Espoused values
Stated: mission, values, "we care 
about the planet". What the 
company says.
Basic assumptions
Unspoken beliefs taken for granted: 
"growth comes first", "cheap is 
smart". They drive real behaviour.

C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N
The say-do gap: stated values vs. lived assumptions
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 7
Espoused value Observed behaviour Underlying assumption
"We care about the planet" Procurement picks the lowest bid every time Cost is the only real measure
"Everyone is a sustainability 
ambassador" No time or budget given for it Sustainability is extra work
"Net zero by 2040" Bonuses depend only on quarterly profit Short-term results come first
"Innovation for good" Failed green pilots are blamed on individuals Risk-taking is unsafe
Staff believe the assumptions, not the posters. Change the assumption by changing what is rewarded and tolerated.

C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N
Culture types and what each means for sustainability
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 8
Culture type (Competing Values) Typical strength Typical sustainability risk
Clan (collaborative) Strong buy-in, shared values, volunteering Groupthink; avoids hard trade-offs
Adhocracy (innovative) Quick pilots, new products and models Pilots without scale or follow-through
Market (results-driven) Clear targets, accountability Only what is measured and monetised 
counts
Hierarchy (rule-based) Reliable compliance and procedures Slow change; compliance mindset
No type is best. Know your starting culture and build on its strengths.

C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N
A maturity ladder for sustainability culture
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 9
Compliance
Meet the rules. Sustainability is a legal 
duty handled by a few specialists.
Programmes
Campaigns and projects run by a 
team. Enthusiasm depends on a few 
people.
Embedded
Built into targets, processes and job 
roles. Staff raise ideas unprompted.
Identity
Part of who we are. Shapes strategy, 
hiring and partnerships.
A teaching model, not a measured standard. Most organisations sit at different levels in different units.

C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N
Why a shared vision matters
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 10
■ Compliance vs. commitment: Senge argues a genuinely 
shared vision creates commitment, whereas imposed goals 
get only compliance.
■ Alignment: a common picture lets teams make consistent 
decisions without constant instruction.
■ Energy: people work harder for a goal they helped shape 
and understand.
■ Direction in conflict: when two good options clash, the 
vision breaks the tie.
■ Risk of the opposite: a slogan written by a consultancy and 
ignored by staff breeds cynicism.
S H A R E D , N O T A N N O U N C E D
A vision is shared when staff can 
describe it in their own words and 
link it to their own work.

C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N
Anatomy of a good vision: the four Cs
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 11
Clear
Simple enough to repeat. 
Specific about where and 
by when.
Credible
Backed by a baseline, a 
plan and leaders' own 
actions.
Compelling
Connects to values 
people care about, not 
only cost.
Connected
Each team can see its 
own part in the whole.

C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N
Worked example: from vision to measurable milestones
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 12
PROBLEM Vision: "Halve the campus's electricity emissions in five years." Baseline 15 GWh/yr, grid factor 0.71 tCO2/MWh, solar yield 
1.4 GWh per MWp (illustrative assumptions).
1. Baseline emissions = 15,000 MWh x 0.71 = 10,650 tCO2 per year
2. Target = 50% cut, so 7.5 GWh avoided (holding the grid factor constant); emissions avoided = 7.5 GWh x 0.71 = 5,325 tCO2
3. Efficiency (LED, controls, behaviour) at 20% of 15 GWh = 3.0 GWh
4. Remaining 7.5 - 3.0 = 4.5 GWh from solar; capacity = 4.5 / 1.4 = 3.2 MWp
5. Milestone: 7.5 / 5 = 1.5 GWh avoided per year, on average, tracked monthly
6. Translate for each block or hostel: share of the 1.5 GWh and a named owner, so the vision becomes a local goal.
A vision becomes shared when each unit can see its own number, and one person owns it.

C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N
Quick check 1
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 13
Staff say, "Management talks green, but we all know the cheapest quote always wins." At which of Schein's 
levels does the real problem sit?
A A. Artifacts
B B. Espoused values
C C. Basic assumptions
D D. None; culture is not layered
Think, vote, then discuss. (Answer in speaker notes.)

C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N
Quick check 1: answer
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 14
Answer: C. Basic assumptions
The espoused value (green) is visible in statements, but the underlying assumption (cheapest wins) drives actual 
procurement. Fix it by changing the evaluation criteria (total cost, supplier data) and by backing a manager who 
chooses a greener, costlier bid.

C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N
Activity: which level of culture?
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 15
Place each observation into one of Schein's levels. Discuss in pairs for 3 minutes.
Artifact
Visible objects, rituals, dashboards, spaces
Espoused value
Stated principles, mission, slogans
Basic assumption
Taken-for-granted, unspoken beliefs
1. "Energy dashboard displayed in the lobby."
2. "Our mission: leave the planet better than we found it."
3. "Of course the plant runs flat out; savings projects can wait."
4. "Monthly zero-waste day with a team prize."
5. "We value people, planet and profit equally" (annual report).
6. "Nobody questions a senior person who ignores the rules."

S E C T I O N 2
Engaging Employees
Employees are not an audience for sustainability communications. They are the people 
who carry it out.
16

E N G A G I N G E M P L O Y E E S
Why employees are central
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 17
■ Scale of decisions: staff make most operational choices: energy use, materials, waste, design 
details.
■ Frontline knowledge: people closest to the process see the waste and the quick fixes.
■ Delivery: targets set at the top are met or missed in teams.
■ Talent: surveys, including Deloitte work on retail workers, link employer sustainability efforts 
with retention and attraction; check findings for your sector.
■ Credibility: employees are also the first to spot greenwashing.

E N G A G I N G E M P L O Y E E S
The engagement spectrum
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 18
Unaware
Does not know or care.
Aware
Knows the goal but does little.
Compliant
Follows rules when asked.
Committed
Acts without being told.
Advocate
Influences others and 
improves the system.
Moving people one step is realistic. A campaign that expects everyone to become an advocate will disappoint.

E N G A G I N G E M P L O Y E E S
What motivates people: self-determination and purpose
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 19
Autonomy
Choice over how to 
contribute. Mandates 
without choice breed 
resentment.
Competence
Feeling able and skilled: 
training, tools, visible 
progress.
Relatedness
Belonging to a team that 
cares: green teams, 
shared goals.
Purpose
Seeing how my work 
links to something bigger.

E N G A G I N G E M P L O Y E E S
The COM-B model: why do people not act?
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 20
Component Question Typical sustainability fix
Capability Do they have the knowledge and skills? Training, simple guides, clear labelling
Opportunity Do the environment and systems make it possible? Bins, bike racks, sub-meters, default settings, time
Motivation Do they want to, and do they believe it matters? Purpose, feedback, recognition, peer norms
Source: Michie, van Stralen and West (2011). Diagnose all three before choosing the intervention.

E N G A G I N G E M P L O Y E E S
Communication: broadcast or dialogue?
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 21
Broadcast only
■ Posters, emails, annual reports
■ One-way, same message for all
■ Measures reach, not understanding
■ Result: awareness without change
Dialogue
■ Town halls, team huddles, Q&A, listening 
sessions
■ Messages adapted to each role
■ Asks what blocks people and acts on it
■ Result: trust and ownership

E N G A G I N G E M P L O Y E E S
Storytelling and framing
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 22
■ Local over global: link climate to the team's own site, 
product or campus.
■ Stories over statistics: one colleague's idea and result is 
remembered longer than a chart.
■ Show the ask: say exactly what each person should do 
next.
■ Frame to values: cost and efficiency for some, health, 
fairness or pride for others.
■ Avoid: guilt and doom as the main message; they trigger 
avoidance.
R E P E A T , V A R Y , S H O W
People need to hear a message 
many times, through different 
channels, and see leaders act on 
it.

E N G A G I N G E M P L O Y E E S
Ways to involve employees
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 23
Green teams
Volunteer cross-functional groups 
that run local projects.
Ideas platform
A simple channel to submit, vote and 
track ideas.
Hackathons
Time-boxed events to solve a real 
sustainability problem.
Town halls
Open Q&A with leaders about 
progress and difficulties.
Ambassadors
Trained peers who explain and 
encourage in their teams.
Volunteering
Community and restoration days 
that build pride and bonds.

E N G A G I N G E M P L O Y E E S
Worked example: campaign vs. default (shut-down 
behaviour)
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 24
PROBLEM 500 office PCs left on overnight draw 60 W for 14 idle hours, 250 working days a year. Tariff Rs 8/kWh, grid factor 0.71 
kgCO2/kWh (illustrative).
1. Waste per PC = 0.060 kW x 14 h x 250 days = 210 kWh per year
2. Fleet waste = 210 x 500 = 105,000 kWh per year
3. Campaign: 60% of staff comply, so saving = 63,000 kWh = Rs 5.04 lakh and 63,000 x 0.71 = 44.7 tCO2
4. Default: auto sleep/shut-down at 95% effectiveness saves 99,750 kWh = Rs 7.98 lakh and 70.8 tCO2
5. The default saves about 58% more than the campaign (99,750 / 63,000 = 1.58), with no ongoing effort.
6. Use engagement for what defaults cannot do: ideas, ownership, and acceptance of the default.
Engagement and system design work together: set the default, then explain why.

E N G A G I N G E M P L O Y E E S
Case: Unilever Sustainable Living Plan
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 25
A C O M P A N Y - W I D E V I S I O N
■ 2010: launched under CEO Paul Polman with goals for health and wellbeing, 
a smaller environmental footprint and better livelihoods.
■ Positioned as a plan for growth, tying the vision to brands and to 
employees' sense of purpose.
■ Replaced in 2020 by the Unilever Compass, a broader strategy.
■ Later reports say some targets were softened or dropped under new 
leadership. Verify the details.
L E S S O N F O R C H A N G E L E A D E R S
A bold, public vision can rally 
employees and attract talent. But if 
the vision is tied to one leader and 
not to systems and incentives, it can 
fade when leadership changes.

E N G A G I N G E M P L O Y E E S
Case: ITC, an Indian triple-bottom-line culture
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 26
T A R G E T S E M B E D D E D I N T H E B U S I N E S S
■ ITC reports being carbon positive, water positive and solid-waste-recycling 
positive for many consecutive years.
■ The goals are set at enterprise level and applied across diverse businesses.
■ Sustainability is presented as part of how the company creates value.
■ Honest critique: the core portfolio includes tobacco, so critics question how 
far such leadership offsets that impact.
■ Check the latest ITC report for current years and figures.
L E S S O N F O R C H A N G E L E A D E R S
Concrete, measurable "positive" 
goals are easy for employees to 
grasp. A credible culture also needs 
honesty about the hardest trade-offs 
in the portfolio.

E N G A G I N G E M P L O Y E E S
Leaders set the culture
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 27
Say
Explain why sustainability 
matters here, in plain 
words, repeatedly.
Do
Visible behaviour: travel 
choices, meeting habits, 
how trade-offs are made.
Fund
Give time, budget and 
authority to the people 
doing the work.
Listen
Seek bad news and 
criticism; act on it 
publicly.

E N G A G I N G E M P L O Y E E S
Middle managers: the squeezed middle
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 28
■ Position: they translate strategy into daily work and carry the targets that conflict.
■ Common problem: told to "be sustainable" but judged only on output and cost.
■ Result: quiet deprioritisation, even when they agree with the goal.
■ What helps: clear targets in their own scorecard, training and a say in how to meet them.
■ Why it matters: staff copy what their immediate manager does and rewards.

E N G A G I N G E M P L O Y E E S
Quick check 2
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 29
Employees at a firm want to cycle to work and know the benefits, but there is no secure bike parking or 
shower. Which COM-B component is the main gap?
A A. Capability
B B. Opportunity
C C. Motivation
D D. None; it is a values problem
Think, vote, then discuss. (Answer in speaker notes.)

E N G A G I N G E M P L O Y E E S
Quick check 2: answer
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 30
Answer: B. Opportunity
Knowledge (capability) and willingness (motivation) are already present. The missing piece is physical: secure parking, 
showers, safe routes. More posters will not help. Provide the facilities, then promote them.

S E C T I O N 3
Embedding in Practice
Moving from words to a way of working: co-creation, rituals, rewards and measurement.
31

E M B E D D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
Co-creating the vision
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 32
Listen
Interviews, surveys and workshops 
across levels and sites.
Draft
A small cross-functional team writes 
options in plain language.
Test
Share drafts, ask "does this feel true? 
what is missing?"
Launch
Leaders commit, with first-year 
milestones and owners.
The process matters as much as the words. A vision people helped write is one they defend.

E M B E D D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
Vision workshop: a half-day format
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 33
Activity Time Output
Current-state reality check: where do we stand, honestly? 30 min Shared fact base and baseline
Future-state story: "It is 2032, what does our campus or site look like?" 45 min Draft images of success
Cluster themes and test against the four Cs 45 min 3-5 vision themes
Barriers and enablers (force-field) 45 min Top obstacles and supports
Commitments: what will each team do in 90 days? 45 min Owners and first actions

E M B E D D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
Rituals, symbols and language
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 34
■ Rituals: a short sustainability item at every team meeting; an annual "green day" with real 
projects.
■ Symbols: who gets the reserved parking, the awards, the stage time; reuse and repair made 
visible.
■ Language: swap "cost of green" for "cost of waste"; make "ask me about carbon" a normal 
sentence.
■ Space: dashboards in common areas, plants, bike racks near the front door.
■ Warning: artifacts without behaviour behind them become jokes.

E M B E D D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
Systems that signal what really matters
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 35
Systems that undermine
■ Hiring and induction never mention 
sustainability
■ Promotions ignore it
■ Travel and procurement rules reward the 
cheapest only
■ Budgets reset yearly, killing multi-year projects
Systems that reinforce
■ Induction includes the vision and each 
person's role
■ Sustainability is in job descriptions and 
appraisals
■ Procurement scores total cost and supplier 
data
■ Protected multi-year funding line

E M B E D D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
Recognition and rewards
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 36
Celebrate teams
Prize the team, share its 
method, not just the 
winner.
Link to appraisal
Include contributions in 
performance reviews and 
promotions.
Reinvest savings
Return part of savings to 
the team for its next 
idea.
Public thanks
Leaders name individuals 
and describe what they 
changed.

E M B E D D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
Inclusive engagement: reach everyone
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 37
■ Frontline and shift workers: often have no email or meeting time; use toolbox talks and 
supervisors.
■ Contract and outsourced staff: cleaners, security, canteen staff touch waste and energy daily; 
include them.
■ Language and literacy: use local languages, pictures and demonstrations.
■ Remote and multi-site teams: do not centre everything at headquarters.
■ Equity link: a culture that excludes workers from decisions contradicts the social side of 
sustainability.

E M B E D D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
Measuring culture: what to track
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 38
Dimension Example indicator Source
Awareness % who can state the vision and their own role Pulse survey
Participation Green team members, ideas submitted and implemented Platform data
Leadership credibility "Leaders act on what they say" (1-5) Pulse survey
Behaviour kWh per head, waste diverted, print volumes Meters, logs
Resources "I have the time and tools to act" (1-5) Pulse survey

E M B E D D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
Worked example: scoring a culture pulse survey
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 39
PROBLEM Five items on a 1-5 scale (mean scores): Awareness 4.2, Personal relevance 3.6, Leadership credibility 2.9, Ability and 
resources 3.1, Peer norms 3.8.
1. Mean score = (4.2 + 3.6 + 2.9 + 3.1 + 3.8) / 5 = 17.6 / 5 = 3.52
2. Convert to a 0-100 index = (3.52 - 1) / 4 x 100 = 63
3. Lowest item: Leadership credibility (2.9). Next lowest: Ability and resources (3.1).
4. Insight: people know and care, but doubt leaders and lack means. More awareness posters would not help.
5. Action: leaders publish and act on one visible commitment; free up time and tools for teams.
6. If credibility rises to 3.9, mean = 18.6 / 5 = 3.72, index = (3.72 - 1) / 4 x 100 = 68.
Read the gaps, not the average: the weakest dimension tells you where to act.

E M B E D D I N G I N P R A C T I C E
Discussion: a shared vision for IIT Delhi hostels
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 40
Scenario: hostel electricity and food waste are rising. Students see no bill, wardens report to different offices, and an 
earlier "green hostel" poster campaign faded in two months.
1 Which level of culture (Schein) is the real problem?
2 Use COM-B: what is missing for students and for staff?
3 Who should co-create the vision, and how?
4 Which default, ritual or reward would you introduce first?

S E C T I O N 4
Sustaining the Culture
Culture is fragile. It is built slowly and can be damaged quickly by one example of 
hypocrisy.
41

S U S T A I N I N G T H E C U L T U R E
Authenticity vs. greenwashing inside the firm
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 42
Signs of internal greenwashing
■ Slogans without budget or owner
■ Targets that quietly move
■ Success stories hide failures
■ Staff are asked to act while leaders fly business 
class
Signs of authenticity
■ Honest reporting of misses
■ Leaders accept trade-offs publicly
■ Resources match ambition
■ Staff criticism is welcomed and acted on

S U S T A I N I N G T H E C U L T U R E
Change fatigue and champion burnout
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 43
■ Too many initiatives: every campaign competes for the same attention.
■ Volunteer overload: green team members do this on top of a full job.
■ Recognition gap: no credit, no time, no budget leads to quiet exit.
■ Remedies: sequence campaigns, count green-team work as part of the role, rotate leadership, 
celebrate wins.
■ Watch: participation falling over time is an early warning of fatigue.

S U S T A I N I N G T H E C U L T U R E
Subcultures, hierarchy and the Indian context
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 44
■ Subcultures: engineering, finance and operations may each interpret sustainability differently; 
speak their languages.
■ Hierarchy: where authority is respected, leaders' visible action carries extra weight, and staff 
may not voice dissent.
■ Frugality as an asset: traditions of reuse and thrift (often called jugaad or "make do") can be 
tapped, but must not be confused with real innovation.
■ Diversity: a single national or global campaign should be adapted by region and site.
■ Caution: these are tendencies, not rules about any person.

S U S T A I N I N G T H E C U L T U R E
Critique: the limits of culture-building
S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y C U L T U R E A N D S H A R E D V I S I O N 45
■ Culture is hard to measure: surveys capture attitudes, and attitudes are not behaviour.
■ Individual responsibility trap: asking staff to switch off lights can distract from large structural 
emissions (energy source, products, supply chain).
■ Weak causal evidence: many engagement claims rest on case studies and self-reports.
■ Manipulation risk: engineered "buy-in" may hide poor decisions or real conflicts of interest.
■ Limits of the firm: culture cannot replace regulation, pricing and infrastructure.

Leadership and Sustainability
Developing leadership skills for driving sustainability within the organisation

Learning outcomes
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 2
■ Define sustainability leadership and distinguish technical from adaptive challenges.
■ Compare transformational, servant, adaptive, ethical and systems leadership.
■ Apply core skills: strategic thinking, influence, negotiation and ethical judgment.
■ Quantify an internal carbon price decision and a 360-degree leadership gap.
■ Plan your own leadership development, and critique the "heroic leader" view.

S E C T I O N 1
Foundations of Leadership
Technology and targets exist. What is scarce is people who can mobilise others to deliver 
them.
4

F O U N D A T I O N S O F L E A D E R S H I P
What is sustainability leadership?
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 5
■ Definition: influencing and enabling others to pursue 
economic, social and environmental goals together, over 
the long term.
■ Not just seniority: leadership is an activity that anyone can 
exercise, from a CEO to a final-year student.
■ Distinctive features: long time horizons, many 
stakeholders, uncertainty and real value conflicts.
■ Research view: Visser and Courtice (2011) review how 
leadership theories apply to sustainability.
K E Y I D E A
Sustainability leaders do not only 
manage projects. They help 
organisations decide what matters 
and mobilise people to act on it.

F O U N D A T I O N S O F L E A D E R S H I P
Leadership styles and what each adds
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 6
Style What it contributes Watch out for
Transformational Inspires a shared vision beyond self-interest Charisma without substance; dependence on 
one person
Servant Puts people and community needs first Slow decisions; may avoid hard calls
Adaptive (Heifetz) Mobilises people to face tough change in values and habits Can unsettle people; needs trust
Ethical / authentic Aligns actions with values; builds credibility Moral certainty that shuts out dissent
Systems Sees interconnections; convenes across boundaries Complexity paralysis; hard to show quick wins
Effective leaders borrow from all of these depending on the situation.

F O U N D A T I O N S O F L E A D E R S H I P
Technical vs. adaptive challenges (Heifetz)
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 7
Technical problem
■ Clear definition, known solution
■ Experts can solve it
■ Example: install LED lighting or rooftop solar
■ Authority and a project plan are enough
Adaptive challenge
■ Problem and solution both unclear
■ People must change habits, loyalties or beliefs
■ Example: departments sharing budgets for a 
joint goal
■ Needs learning, dialogue and experiment

F O U N D A T I O N S O F L E A D E R S H I P
Systems leadership: three core capabilities
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 8
See the larger system
Help people from different 
organisations understand the whole, 
beyond their own part.
Foster reflection
Create conversations where people 
listen, reflect and rethink their 
assumptions.
Co-create the future
Shift from reacting to problems to 
building shared options for the 
future.

F O U N D A T I O N S O F L E A D E R S H I P
Key competencies for sustainability (Wiek et al.)
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 9
Systems 
thinking
Analyse links across 
scales and sectors.
Anticipatory
Envision and assess 
possible futures.
Normative
Judge goals and 
trade-offs against 
values.
Strategic
Design and 
implement change 
that works.
Interpersonal
Collaborate, 
negotiate and build

F O U N D A T I O N S O F L E A D E R S H I P
The inner side of leadership
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 10
Values
Clarity about what you 
will not trade away.
Long-term 
thinking
Willingness to accept 
costs now for benefits 
you may not see.
Humility
Admit what you do not

with less power.
Moral courage

F O U N D A T I O N S O F L E A D E R S H I P
Four levels of leadership
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 11
Self
Understand your values, strengths 
and blind spots; model the behaviour.
Team
Build trust, set goals, create space for 
ideas and dissent.
Organisation
Shape strategy, structures, incentives 
and culture.
Ecosystem
Work with suppliers, regulators, peers 
and communities.
Sustainability challenges rarely respect organisational boundaries, so leaders must work at all four levels.

F O U N D A T I O N S O F L E A D E R S H I P
Quick check 1
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 12
A university wants every department to share one energy budget so that savings can be reinvested. 
Departments refuse, fearing loss of control. This is mainly a:
A A. Technical problem needing a better meter
B B. Adaptive challenge needing dialogue and changed assumptions
C C. Compliance problem needing a stricter rule
D D. Data problem needing more surveys
Think, vote, then discuss. (Answer in speaker notes.)

F O U N D A T I O N S O F L E A D E R S H I P
Quick check 1: answer
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 13
Answer: B. An adaptive challenge
The technology and the arithmetic are known. The obstacle is how people feel about losing control and trusting a 
shared pool. A leader must convene departments, surface fears, test small shared-budget pilots and build trust. Forcing 
the rule alone may bring compliance but little commitment.

F O U N D A T I O N S O F L E A D E R S H I P
Activity: technical or adaptive?
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 14
Place each challenge into a bucket. Discuss in pairs for 3 minutes.
Technical
Known fix; experts and a plan can solve it
Adaptive
People must change habits, beliefs or 
relationships
Mixed
Technical solution plus adaptive barrier
1. "Replace diesel generators with a solar-battery system."
2. "Engineers and sales disagree about what customers value in repairable products."
3. "Cut data-centre energy use by tuning cooling."
4. "Suppliers resist sharing emissions data."
5. "Senior staff refuse to give up business-class travel."
6. "Switch the canteen to a reusable crockery system."

S E C T I O N 2
Core Leadership Skills
A practical toolkit: seeing the long term, deciding under uncertainty, influencing others 
and acting ethically.
15

C O R E L E A D E R S H I P S K I L L S
Vision and purpose: leading with meaning
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 16
■ Why it matters: people follow a purpose they understand and believe in.
■ Link to culture: a vision is shared only when co-created; leaders start the conversation, not 
finish it.
■ Be specific: name the outcome, the date, the owner and what will be given up.
■ Stay consistent: decisions under pressure show whether the purpose is real.
■ Say it simply: if a mid-level manager cannot repeat it, it will not guide choices.

C O R E L E A D E R S H I P S K I L L S
Strategic thinking across three time horizons
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 17
Horizon Focus Leader's question
Now (0-2 years) Efficiency, compliance, quick wins Are we doing the basics well, and showing results?
Next (2-5 years) New products, processes and capabilities What must we build now to be competitive then?
Beyond (5-15 years) Business model and system change What world are we preparing for, and what is our 
role?
Balance all three. A portfolio of only Horizon 1 projects is safe but strategically weak.

C O R E L E A D E R S H I P S K I L L S
Worked example: an internal carbon price
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 18
PROBLEM Replace a boiler. Option A: gas boiler, capex Rs 50 lakh, opex Rs 10 lakh/yr, 800 tCO2/yr. Option B: electric heat pump, capex 
Rs 80 lakh, opex Rs 6 lakh/yr, 400 tCO2/yr. 10 years, 10% discount rate (illustrative).
1. Annuity factor (10 years, 10%) = 6.1446
2. No carbon price: PV(A) = 50 + 10 x 6.1446 = Rs 111.4 lakh; PV(B) = 80 + 6 x 6.1446 = Rs 116.9 lakh. A looks cheaper by Rs 5.4
lakh.
3. With Rs 2,000/tCO2: carbon cost A = 800 x 2,000 = Rs 16 lakh/yr; B = Rs 8 lakh/yr.
4. PV(A) = 111.4 + 16 x 6.1446 = Rs 209.8 lakh; PV(B) = 116.9 + 8 x 6.1446 = Rs 166.0 lakh. B is cheaper by Rs 43.7 lakh.
5. Break-even price = 5.42 lakh / (400 t x 6.1446) = about Rs 221 per tonne.
6. Leaders use the price as a decision tool, not as a tax: it makes a hidden cost visible.
Even a small carbon price flips this decision. The leader's job is to make the cost visible and to decide with it.

C O R E L E A D E R S H I P S K I L L S
Influencing without authority
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 19
Build coalitions
Find allies in finance, 
operations and the front 
line before the big 
meeting.
Frame for 
interests
Speak in terms of each 
person's goals: cost, risk, 
pride, growth.
Use evidence
Numbers and a short 
story from a credible 
pilot.
Start with a pilot
Lower the risk; let results 
persuade sceptics.

C O R E L E A D E R S H I P S K I L L S
Stakeholders, negotiation and trade-offs
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 20
■ Investors: want returns and risk control; show the link to 
value.
■ Regulators: want compliance and transparency; engage 
early.
■ Employees and unions: want security and fairness in a 
transition.
■ Communities: bear local impacts; consult and share 
benefits.
■ Negotiation approach: identify interests behind positions, 
create options for mutual gain, and be clear about non￾negotiables.
T R A D E -O F F S A R E N O R M A L
Cost vs. emissions, jobs vs. 
closure, speed vs. fairness. Make 
the trade-off explicit and explain 
the choice.

C O R E L E A D E R S H I P S K I L L S
Communication and storytelling for leaders
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 21
■ Start with why: explain the purpose before the plan.
■ Be honest: share setbacks and uncertainty, not only wins.
■ Tell stories: one concrete example moves people more than a slide of statistics.
■ Listen more than you speak: ask what blocks people; act on what you hear.
■ Tailor: adjust language for the board, the plant floor and the public.
■ Avoid: doom, jargon and green claims you cannot back with evidence.

C O R E L E A D E R S H I P S K I L L S
Ethical judgment: common dilemmas and questions to ask
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 22
Dilemma Questions a leader asks
Cost vs. environmental performance What is the full cost, including future risk? Who bears the harm if we choose 
cheaper?
Jobs vs. closing a polluting plant Is there a just-transition plan? Have affected workers been consulted?
Marketing claims vs. evidence Can we prove it? Would we be comfortable if a journalist checked?
Speed vs. consultation Who is missing from the decision? What do we lose by rushing?

C O R E L E A D E R S H I P S K I L L S
Resilience: leading through setbacks
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 23
■ Expect resistance and failure: pilots fail, budgets get cut, allies leave.
■ Separate setback from purpose: learn from the failure, keep the goal.
■ Protect energy: sustainability work can feel endless and emotionally heavy; share the load, 
rest, and celebrate progress.
■ Build support: peer networks, mentors and a coalition reduce burnout.
■ Model it: teams copy how leaders respond to bad news.

C O R E L E A D E R S H I P S K I L L S
Partnerships: transactional or transformative?
L E A D E R S H I P F O R S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y 24
Transactional
■ Donation or one-off sponsorship
■ Brand benefit is the main goal
■ Short projects, unclear impact
■ Partners meet rarely
Transformative
■ Shared goals and joint resources
■ Both sides change how they work
■ Multi-year, with learning built in
■ Trust built through regular dialogue
